parts.problem_md:
The following equation represents the melting of ice.

H<sub>2</sub>O (s) → H<sub>2</sub>O (l)            ∆*H*<sup>ϴ</sup> = +6.03 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>    ∆*S*<sup>ϴ</sup> = +22.1 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>

State the meaning of the symbol <sup>ϴ</sup> in ∆*H*<sup>ϴ</sup>.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The meaning of the symbol <sup>⊖</sup> in Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> is:
> 
> - Standard conditions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The <sup>⊖</sup> symbol indicates that the value was measured under standard conditions: a pressure of 101 kPa and a temperature of 298 K (25 °C).

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The following equation represents the melting of ice.

H~2~O (s) → H~2~O (l)            ∆*H*^ϴ^ = +6.03 kJ mol^–1^    ∆*S*^ϴ^ = +22.1 J K^–1^ mol^–1^

Explain why the standard entropy change for this process is positive.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The standard entropy change is positive because:
> 
> - A liquid is formed from a solid / ice melts to form liquid water **[1 mark]**
> - Liquid water is more disordered than solid ice / particles have greater freedom of movement in a liquid than in a solid **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Entropy is a measure of disorder in a system. The greater the disorder, the higher the entropy.
> 
> In this process, ice (a solid) changes to liquid water. Particles in a liquid have greater freedom of movement than those in a solid, so the system becomes more disordered and entropy increases, making Δ*S*<sup>⊖</sup> positive.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The following equation represents the melting of ice.

H₂O (s) → H₂O (l)            ∆H° = +6.03 kJ mol⁻¹    ∆S° = +22.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

Calculate the temperature at which ∆*G*<sup>ϴ</sup> = 0 for this process.

Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the temperature at which Δ*G*<sup>⊖</sup> = 0:

- List the known values:

  - Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> = +6.03 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*S*<sup>⊖</sup> = +22.1 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Rearrange Δ*G*<sup>⊖</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>⊖</sup> = 0 to find *T*:

*T* = `\frac{\Delta H^{\ominus}}{\Delta S^{\ominus}}` **[1 mark]**

- Convert Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> from kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> to J mol<sup>−1</sup> and substitute:

*T* = $\frac{6.03\times1000}{22.1}$ **[1 mark]**

*T* = **273 K** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct rearrangement: *T* = Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> ÷ Δ*S*<sup>⊖</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with consistent units (Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> converted to J mol<sup>−1</sup>, or Δ*S*<sup>⊖</sup> converted to kJ K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct answer: 273 K

> **[exam-tip]**
> When using the Gibbs equation, Δ*H* and Δ*S* must be in the same units. Here, Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> is in kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>⊖</sup> is in J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>, so you must convert one to match the other before dividing.
> 
> The simplest approach is to multiply Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> by 1000 to convert to J mol<sup>−1</sup>: 6.03 x 1000 = 6030 J mol<sup>−1</sup>.
> 
> Alternatively, divide Δ*S*<sup>⊖</sup> by 1000 to convert to kJ K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>: 22.1 ÷ 1000 = 0.0221 kJ K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>. Both approaches give *T* = 273 K, which is 0 °C, the melting point of ice.

parts.problem_md:
Ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, is produced by the Haber process and is an important chemical in the manufacture of fertilisers and cleaning products.

Ammonia gas can react with oxygen to produce nitrogen monoxide and steam, and is the first step in the Ostwald process which produces nitric acid.

i) Construct an equation for the reaction of ammonia with oxygen to produce nitrogen monoxide and steam.

[2]

ii) Standard entropies are shown in Table 2.1.

**Table 2.1**

| **substance** | **entropy values (J K**<sup>**-1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>**)** |
|---|---|
| NH<sub>3</sub> (g) | 192.8 |
| O<sub>2</sub> (g) | 205.2 |
| H<sub>2</sub>O (g) | 188.8 |
| NO (g) | 210.8 |

Calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction at 298 K.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
i) The balanced equation for the reaction of ammonia with oxygen is:

4NH<sub>3</sub> (g) + 5O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 4NO (g) + 6H<sub>2</sub>O (g)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants, products and balancing
> 
> 1 mark for all correct state symbols

ii) To calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction:

- Apply Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants):

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = [(4 x Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(NO (g))) + (6 x Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(H<sub>2</sub>O (g)))] − [(4 x Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(NH<sub>3</sub> (g))) + (5 x Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(O<sub>2</sub> (g)))] **[1 mark]**

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = [(4 x 210.8) + (6 x 188.8)] − [(4 x 192.8) + (5 x 205.2)]

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = [843.2 + 1132.8] − [771.2 + 1026.0]

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 1976.0 − 1797.2

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **+178.8 J K**<sup>**−1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**−1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct method: ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants) with stoichiometric coefficients correctly applied
> 
> 1 mark for the correct answer: +178.8 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The equation to calculate entropy change is:
> 
> Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants)
> 
> Don't forget to multiply each standard entropy value by the stoichiometric coefficient of that species in the balanced equation. This balancing step must be carried through the entire calculation.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Ammonia gas can react with oxygen to produce nitrogen monoxide and steam, and is the first step in the Ostwald process which produces nitric acid.

i) Construct an equation for the reaction of ammonia with oxygen to produce nitrogen monoxide and steam.

The balanced equation for the reaction of ammonia with oxygen is:

4NH3 (g) + 5O2 (g) → 4NO (g) + 6H2O (g)

Explain why the standard entropy change for the reaction in **(a)** is positive.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The standard entropy change is positive because:
> 
> - There are 10 moles of gas in the products
> **AND**
> 9 moles of gas in the reactants
> **OR**
> There are more moles of gas in the products than in the reactants
> **OR**
> The system becomes more disordered **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Examiners noted that many candidates did not explicitly state the change in moles of gaseous species. For full credit, state both the number of moles of gas in the products and the number in the reactants: 10 moles of gas on the right and 9 moles of gas on the left means the system becomes more disordered, giving a positive Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Standard entropies are shown in Table 2.1.

**Table 2.1**

| **substance** | **entropy values (J K**^**-1**^** mol**^**-1**^**)** |
| :---: | :---: |
| NH~3~ (g) | 192.8 |
| O~2~ (g) | 205.2 |
| H~2~O (g) | 188.8 |
| NO (g) | 210.8 |

The second step in the Ostwald process produces nitrogen dioxide as shown in the equation

2NO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g)             Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −112 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

The standard entropy of NO<sub>2</sub> (g) is 240.0 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>.

i) Use Table 2.1 to calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction at 298 K.

[2]

ii) Use your answer to (c)(i) to calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction at 298 K. Show your working.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
i) To calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for the reaction 2NO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g):

- Apply Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants):

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = [2 x Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(NO<sub>2</sub> (g))] − [(2 x Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(NO (g))) + Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(O<sub>2</sub> (g))] **[1 mark]**

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = (2 x 240.0) − [(2 x 210.8) + 205.2]

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 480.0 − [421.6 + 205.2]

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 480.0 − 626.8

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **−146.8 J K**<sup>**−1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**−1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct method: ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants) with stoichiometric coefficients correctly applied
> 
> 1 mark for the correct answer: −146.8 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>

ii) To calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction at 298 K:

- List the known values:

  - Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −112 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = −146.8 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> (from (c)(i))
  - *T* = 298 K
- State the Gibbs equation:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> and substitute:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −112 − (298 x −0.1468) **[1 mark]**

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −112 + 43.7

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = **−68.3 kJ mol**<sup>**−1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for stating the Gibbs equation: Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with consistent units
> 
> 1 mark for the correct answer: −68.3 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect value of Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> in (c)(i)

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), the entropy change is negative because the number of moles of gas decreases: 3 moles of gas on the left (2NO + O<sub>2</sub>) become 2 moles on the right (2NO<sub>2</sub>). Fewer moles of gas means less disorder, so Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is negative.
> 
> For part (ii), remember to convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> to kJ K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> before substituting into the Gibbs equation, since Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> is given in kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. Divide Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> by 1000: −146.8 ÷ 1000 = −0.1468 kJ K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>.

parts.problem_md:
Potassium nitrate is a soluble salt. When it dissolves in water the value of the enthalpy change Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = +34.9 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> and the value of the entropy change Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = +117 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>.

Construct an equation, including state symbols, for the process that occurs when potassium nitrate dissolves in water.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for potassium nitrate dissolving in water is:
> 
> - KNO<sub>3</sub> (s) → K<sup>+</sup> (aq) + NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> (aq)
> **OR**
> KNO<sub>3</sub> (s) + aq → K<sup>+</sup> (aq) + NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The standard enthalpy change of solution (Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub>) is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of an ionic substance dissolves in sufficient water to form a very dilute solution.
> 
> The symbol (aq) indicates that the ions are dissolved in sufficient water to form a dilute aqueous solution.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Potassium nitrate is a soluble salt. When it dissolves in water the value of the enthalpy change Δ*H*^θ^ = +34.9 kJ mol^−1^ and the value of the entropy change Δ*S*^θ^ = +117 J K^−1^ mol^−1^.

Construct an equation, including state symbols, for the process that occurs when potassium nitrate dissolves in water.

KNO~3~ (s) → K^+^ (aq) + NO~3~^−^ (aq)

Explain why Δ*S*<sup>θ </sup>is positive for this process.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is positive because:
> 
> - Disorder increases as the solid dissolves / solid changes to aqueous ions / particles have greater freedom of movement in solution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When KNO<sub>3</sub> dissolves, the ionic lattice breaks down:
> 
> KNO<sub>3</sub> (s) → K<sup>+</sup> (aq) + NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> (aq)
> 
> The ions are now free to move in solution, so disorder increases and entropy increases, making Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> positive.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Potassium nitrate is a soluble salt. When it dissolves in water the value of the enthalpy change Δ*H*^θ^ = +34.9 kJ mol^−1^ and the value of the entropy change Δ*S*^θ^ = +117 J K^−1^ mol^−1^.

Calculate the temperature above which the dissolving of potassium nitrate becomes feasible. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the temperature above which the dissolving of potassium nitrate becomes feasible:

- List the known values:

  - Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = +34.9 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = +117 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>
- At the feasibility threshold, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0. Rearrange Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 0 to find *T*:

*T* = $\frac{ΔH^{θ}}{ΔS^{θ}}$ **[1 mark]**

- Convert Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> from kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> to J mol<sup>−1</sup> and substitute:

*T* = $\frac{34.9\times1000}{117}$ **[1 mark]**

*T* = **298 K** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct rearrangement: *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> ÷ Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with consistent units
> 
> 1 mark for the correct answer: 298 K

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction becomes feasible when Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> ≤ 0. Setting Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0 gives the threshold temperature above which the reaction becomes feasible.
> 
> Remember to ensure Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> are in the same units before dividing. Here, multiply Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> by 1000 to convert from kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> to J mol<sup>−1</sup>: 34.9 x 1000 = 34 900 J mol<sup>−1</sup>. Then divide by Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 117 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> to get *T* = 298 K.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Potassium nitrate is a soluble salt. When it dissolves in water the value of the enthalpy change ΔH^θ = +34.9 kJ mol^−1^ and the value of the entropy change ΔS^θ = +117 J K^−1^ mol^−1^.

Calculate the temperature above which the dissolving of potassium nitrate becomes feasible.

T = ΔH^θ ÷ ΔS^θ
T = (34.9 × 1000) ÷ 117
T = 298 K

i) State the sign of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> for this process at a temperature lower than your answer to part (c).

[1]

ii) State what this value of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> indicates about the dissolving of potassium nitrate at this lower temperature.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The sign of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> at a temperature lower than 298 K:
> 
> - Positive / Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> > 0 **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A positive Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> indicates that:
> 
> - The dissolving of potassium nitrate is not feasible / not spontaneous / does not occur at this temperature **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow error carried forward from (d)(i): if negative, allow "feasible / spontaneous"

> **[exam-tip]**
> At the threshold temperature from part (c), Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0. Below this temperature, the *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> term decreases in magnitude, so Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> becomes more positive.
> 
> A positive Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> means the process is not feasible: potassium nitrate is less likely to dissolve at temperatures below 298 K.

parts.problem_md:
Fig. 3.1 shows how entropy changes with temperature.

![Graph showing entropy plotted against temperature for water, with stepwise increases at two phase transition temperatures T1 and T2, representing melting and boiling respectively](assets/001-graph-showing-entropy-plotted-against-temperatur.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

i) The entropy of water is zero when the temperature is zero Kelvin. Explain this in terms of the arrangement and motion of the water molecules.

[2]

ii) Explain why the entropy change, Δ*S*, is larger at temperature *T*<sub>2</sub> than at temperature *T*<sub>1</sub>.

[2]

iii) Label the boiling point, *T*<sub>b</sub>, on the appropriate axis.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
iii) The completed figure is:

![Entropy versus temperature graph for water with the boiling point Tb marked on the temperature axis, vertically below the step at T2](assets/002-entropy-versus-temperature-graph-for-water-with-.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) At 0 K, the entropy of water is zero because:
> 
> - (At 0 K) particles are stationary / not moving / not vibrating
> **OR**
> The particles have zero kinetic energy **[1 mark]**
> - There is no disorder / perfect order / maximum order in the arrangement of the particles **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The entropy change is larger at *T*<sub>2</sub> than at *T*<sub>1</sub> because:
> 
> - *T*<sub>2</sub> corresponds to boiling / evaporating / condensing / l → g / g → l
> **AND**
> *T*<sub>1</sub> corresponds to melting / freezing / s → l / l → s **[1 mark]**
> - The change in disorder is greater for *T*<sub>2</sub> / boiling than for *T*<sub>1</sub> / melting **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) 1 mark for *T*<sub>b</sub> marked on the temperature axis, vertically below the second step, *T*<sub>2</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> When explaining the entropy change from Fig. 3.1, compare the change in state with the change in disorder to gain both marks.
> 
> Avoid discussing the change in disorder without clearly stating the change in state — for example, specify a change from liquid to gas, not just 'gas'.
> 
> The boiling point represents the largest change in entropy, as the state changes from liquid to gas. This is why *T*<sub>b</sub> is marked on the temperature axis, vertically below *T*<sub>2</sub> on Fig. 3.1.

parts.problem_md:
Standard entropies can be used to calculate the entropy change of a reaction, Δ*S*. For example, for the reaction between nitrogen monoxide and ozone.

NO (g) + O<sub>3</sub> (g) → NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g)

Standard entropy values are shown in Table 3.1

**Table 3.1**

| **Substance** | **Entropy value / J K**<sup>-1</sup>** mol**<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| NO (g) | 210.8 |
| O<sub>2</sub> (g) | 205.2 |
| NO<sub>2</sub> (g) | 240.0 |
| O<sub>3</sub> (g) | 238.9 |

Using Table 3.1, calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> of the reaction between nitrogen monoxide and ozone at 298 K. Show your working.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
To calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for the reaction:

- Apply the formula Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup> (products) – Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup> (reactants):

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = (240.0 + 205.2) – (210.8 + 238.9) **[1 mark]**

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 445.2 – 449.7

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **–4.5 J K**<sup>**–1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct formula and substitution: (240.0 + 205.2) – (210.8 + 238.9)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct final answer: –4.5 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> When calculating the standard entropy change of a reaction, use the formula:
> 
> Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup> (products) – Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup> (reactants)
> 
> Remember to account for the number of moles of each substance in the balanced equation when applying this formula.

parts.problem_md:
The contact process is a method used industrially to form sulfur trioxide, by reacting sulfur dioxide and oxygen together over a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst.

The equation for this reaction is shown below:

2SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2SO<sub>3</sub> (g)

Enthalpy of formation values are shown in Table 3.2

**Table 3.2**

| **Substance** | **Formation enthalpy values (kJ mol**<sup>-1</sup>**)** |
|---|---|
| SO<sub>2</sub> (g) | –297 |
| SO<sub>3</sub> (g) | –395 |

i) Using Table 3.2, calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, using the data provided. Show your working.

[2]

ii) The standard entropy change of this reaction is –189 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>. Use this value and your enthalpy value from part (i) to calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction at 298 K. Show your working.

[3]

iii) Use your answer to part (ii) to state whether the reaction is feasible at 298 K.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) To calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction:

- Apply the formula:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> (products) – ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> (reactants)

**OR**

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = (2 x –395) – (2 x –297) **[1 mark]**

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = –790 – (–594)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = **–196 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for the formula **AND** correct substitution: (2 × –395) – (2 × –297)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct final answer: –196 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Writing out the formula at the start of a calculation can sometimes earn the first mark, and is good practice for structuring your working.

ii) To calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change at 298 K:

- Convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = –189 ÷ 1000 = –0.189 kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Apply the formula:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> – *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>

**OR**

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = –196 – (298 x –0.189) **[1 mark]**

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = **–140 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
>
